data.title: Gars-Thunau – a Great Moravian hillfort in Austria
data.excerpt: The power of the Great Moravian princes reached beyond Moravia, Slovakia and Bohemia into a considerable part of what is now Austria, and Gars-Thunau in the Kamptal is the best known of the Great Moravian hillforts there. A charter of 902/903 names the Slavic prince Joseph as its likely lord, while excavation between 1965 and 1990 revealed a princely court behind a palisade, a timber-and-earth rampart in two building phases and a southern gateway reconstructed as a multi-storey tower.

keyFacts.value: On Obere Holzwiese, bounded by a palisade fence that was rebuilt three times

keyFacts.label: Rampart – later phase
keyFacts.value: Chambered construction with a stone front wall, height up to 4 m, wall-walk width 4–4.5 m

children.text: The power of the Great Moravian princes, as is well known, extended not only over the territory of Moravia, Slovakia and Bohemia, but also over the territory of several neighbouring countries. It may surprise some that a considerable part of present-day Austria also belonged to Great Moravia. The evidence for this consists of several Great Moravian hillforts in Austria, of which the best known is Gars-Thunau.

The first historical mention of the site is in a donation charter of the monastery of Freising. It records that in 902/903 the Slavic prince Joseph gave part of his property in the Kamptal into the hands of the bishop of the monastery at Freising in Bavaria, for the good of his soul. This otherwise unknown prince was certainly also the lord of the Slavic hillfort between the present-day towns of Gars and Thunau in the Kamptal. The first interest in the site thus came from historians, and the first investigations by amateur archaeologists did not take long to follow. In the last third of the 19th century Johann Krahuletz demonstrated the Slavic origin of the surviving occupation when he discovered an extensive early medieval cemetery here. Various investigations were subsequently carried out, but these were of a rather collector-driven character. In the 1930s the first professional excavation was then undertaken. The excavation begun in 1965 went on to demonstrate the massive scale of the hillfort's fortification and its extent, and it ended 25 years later, in 1990.
The site and the Slavic occupation

blocks.alt: Gars-Thunau – a Great Moravian hillfort in Austria

children.text:
The fortified Slavic hillfort lay in the Kamptal, between the towns of Gars am Kamp and Thunau am Kamp in Lower Austria. The settlement spreads over a rise, today densely wooded, near the River Kamp. This location is fundamental in historical terms, because it lies on the eastern periphery of East Francia and in the north is in direct contact with Moravia, which strongly influenced the fortunes of the hillfort. The character of the find material clearly demonstrates the influence of Moravia.
 
 The site on which the early medieval hillfort of Gars-Thunau lies is very well placed strategically. The rise offers ample space for a rich settlement structure. At the same time the higher position gave the hillfort good defensive conditions. Not only did the inhabitants have a good overview of events across a wide landscape from this position, but the builders of the early medieval fortification also made ingenious use of the topographical situation of the promontory and thereby markedly increased the defensive capacity of the hillfort.

On the extensive promontory, several areas in which traces of early medieval occupation were uncovered were distinguished during the systematic excavation. To the west lies the so-called Schanze (the Redoubt). This almost rectangular area is bounded on three sides by an early medieval rampart; on the east the space is open and connected by a rocky neck with the rest of the hillfort. Entrances into the Schanze area were uncovered in the northern and southern ramparts. To the west of the Schanze burial mounds were found, and to the east there then extends a large area called Obere Holzwiese (the Upper Wood Meadow). Obere Holzwiese runs out to the south into a tip of the rise, which falls away sharply into the valley and, as on the northern side, is enclosed by an early medieval rampart. On the east the Obere Holzwiese area then passes into a further part of the hillfort, designated Unter Holzwiese (the Lower Wood Meadow). This area closes off the early medieval part of the hillfort, again by means of a pronounced northern rampart. On the southern side no fortification was identified, which may be connected with the steep terrain, which could have offered sufficient protection. A gateway is presumed at the north-eastern corner of the site, but it has not been demonstrated archaeologically. The last and northernmost part of the hill is the Nordhang (the North Slope), an extensive bailey where burial mounds were uncovered; it no longer falls within the fortified part of the hillfort, even though traces of occupation have been observed here.

children.text: The hillfort was already occupied in prehistory and antiquity. The arrival of the first Slavs at the site of Gars-Thunau can be dated to the first half of the 9th century. The settlers visibly made use of the natural protection of the ruined Final Bronze Age fortification and settled at the spur of the southern rampart, which was formed in the shape of a V. Not long afterwards, at the beginning of the second half of the 9th century, a

enclosed by a palisade had already been built. At the same time the construction of an extensive timber-and-earth fortification was also begun here. The question remains whether the other two areas (Schanze and Unter Holzwiese), which are enclosed by a rampart together with Obere Holzwiese, were joined to this area at the same time, or were occupied and fortified subsequently. Around the middle of the 10th century the hillfort slowly lost its importance (probably as a result of the political and economic changes that came about at the hillfort after the defeat in the fighting with the Magyars), and in the second half of the 10th century we then find the last traces of occupation on Obere Holzwiese.

The fortification of the hillfort of Gars-Thunau encloses an extensive area measuring 140 m across on the north–south axis and 600 m on the west–east axis. This complex comprised three parts. The westernmost part, the Schanze, served as an advanced defensive stronghold, while Obere and Unter Holzwiese were the place of the occupation proper, with buildings; at the Obere Holzwiese site there stood — as has already been mentioned — a

bounded by a palisade fence. As the bedding trenches in the subsoil show, this palisade fence was altered three times and each time enclosed an area of a different size. Between the Schanze and Obere Holzwiese areas the original Final Bronze Age rampart is still visible today. The early medieval circuit fortification, however, was probably not built around the entire perimeter of the hillfort area. There is no doubt about its existence in the Schanze area and the adjoining northern and western part of Obere Holzwiese. In other places the natural terrain was used, as for example on the southern slope of Obere Holzwiese. At the south-eastern edge of Obere Holzwiese, by contrast, use was made of a swell on the ground formed by the remains of the Final Bronze Age fortification. It seems that this rampart was faced with stones on its front side in order to increase its defensive capacity. A provisional rampart with a stone wall was created here, since a stronger fortification was evidently not necessary given the sharp drop into the valley. In the Unter Holzwiese area the fortification was not detected archaeologically to any marked degree, but it may be assumed that a timber-and-earth rampart stood in the north, including an eastern entrance gateway. The timber-and-earth rampart of the hillfort went through two building phases. These alterations concerned not only the construction of the structure but above all the area that the rampart delimited. The rampart of the earlier phase had a grillage construction with no stone used at the front of the rampart; the later phase was represented by a rampart of chambered (box) construction with a stone front wall.

children.text: The fortification at the western Schanze site was formed in the shape of the letter U, with the area on the eastern side left open. The total extent of the Schanze area was 100 × 170 m, and it was interpreted as the main advanced place of defence, the rampart here protecting the easily accessible entrance to the hillfort. The two natural terraces, Obere and Unter Holzwiese, form a unit enclosed by the northern and southern stretches of the fortification. These two ramparts are independent of each other and their ruins are less visible today than in the case of the Schanze area. The northern fortification is considerably longer than the southern one, while their construction remains the same as in the case of the fortification on the Schanze. As already stated above, the southern fortification did not have to be built given the landscape situation, and the ruins of the Early Bronze Age fortification served the inhabitants sufficiently for protective effect.

blocks.alt: Gars-Thunau – a Great Moravian hillfort in Austria

children.text: To the east of the southern gateway a stretch was found in which a trench uncovered the earlier early medieval fortification. A system of round logs, which overlapped in log-cabin fashion and were not joined with nails, survived to a height of one metre. This was a grillage construction, which formed regular square spaces measuring 1.5 × 1.5 m. The empty spaces were filled with stone of local origin and with soil. No traces of a stone wall were found on the front side. The rampart of the later phase was formed by a chambered construction. The chambers were formed of unworked trunks with their bark, and log-cabin technique was used to tie them together, again without the use of reinforcement with nails. The longitudinal wall of a chamber was formed by trunks 7 m long, and across them were laid transverse trunks about 5 m long, at a distance of 2.4 m from one another. Further transverse trunks rested on these, and further storeys of the construction were thus created. The transverse trunks, however, reached approximately 1 m of their length into the construction of the stone front facing and partly also projected on the rear side of the rampart. The spaces of the chambers were filled with soil and stone. In front of the front wall of the chambers there was a massive stone layer, which reached a width of 1.5 to 2 m. Overall, therefore, the width of the base of the rampart was approximately 7 m.

blocks.alt: Gars-Thunau – a Great Moravian hillfort in Austria

children.text: In the western stretch at the Schanze site, small rectangular buildings with a corner hearth were uncovered, probably built using the block technique. The buildings abutted directly on the rear wall of the rampart and stood at regular intervals of 5 m. In the north-eastern corner of the Schanze site a depression in the rampart was uncovered, which was interpreted as the entrance into the area of the hillfort. The wings of the rampart turned inwards towards the interior of the hillfort here, the right wing being somewhat longer than the left. The depression between them was 4.2 m across and 5 m long. In the middle a row of small round pits was uncovered, which divided the space into halves. In the southern rampart, almost opposite the northern gateway, a further entrance into the hillfort was uncovered. The entrance was again between two wings of the rampart, but was of considerably smaller dimensions.

On the outer side the rampart could have reached a height of up to 4 m (without the palisade on the crest of the rampart body). The width of the wall-walk on the top of the rampart was around 4 m to 4.5 m. A notable feature of the western stretch of the fortification are the rectangular timber buildings with a hearth, which stand on the inner side of the rampart at regular intervals. These features are interpreted as cabins built using the block technique. Such adjoining dwellings are no exception in the Early Middle Ages, and houses built directly against the inner wall of the rampart could have helped to reduce the pressure exerted on the rear wall of the rampart by its earthen fill.

blocks.alt: Gars-Thunau – a Great Moravian hillfort in Austria

children.text: On the basis of the find situation, a situational reconstruction of the southern gateway was produced. It is shown as a multi-storey tower. The lower chamber represented the entrance into the hillfort, reached the same height as the height of the rampart, and its width was identical with the distance between the two inturned wings of the gateway. At the level of the wall-walk there was then a further storey of the gateway, and above it a tower. Access from the first storey of the gateway is by means of a ladder through the floor of the tower, where the opening is protected on both sides by a railing. At the level of the wall-walk a chamber is built across the whole width of the entrance. From it the already proposed access to the tower is possible. The chamber is completely boarded with timber; the only open space is an embrasure, loopholes and passages for moving from one side of the wall-walk to the other. The wall-walk itself in the vicinity of the gateway is covered by a breastwork. The vertical beams are approximately 0.6 m apart. Their height reaches 2 m and they are pointed at the top. Between the vertical beams, planks are laid horizontally. These alternately reach heights of 1.2 and 1.8 m and thus form a protective screen in the form of crenellation.

blocks.alt: Gars-Thunau – a Great Moravian hillfort in Austria

children.text: In the first half of the 10th century the hillfort fell victim to an attack, probably by the Magyars. The occupation — now of an agricultural character — moved to the area of the unfortified Untere Holzwiese, where it then continued until the middle of the 11th century.
